In [[mathematics]], the term '''permutation representation''' of a (typically finite) [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> can refer to either of two closely related notions: a [[representation (mathematics)|representation]] of <math>G</math> as a group of [[permutation]]s, or as a group of [[permutation matrices]]. The term also refers to the combination of the two.

==Abstract permutation representation==
A '''permutation representation''' of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> on a [[set (mathematics)|set]] <math>X</math> is a [[group homomorphism|homomorphism]] from <math>G</math> to the [[symmetric group]] of <math>X</math>:

: <math>\rho\colon G \to \operatorname{Sym}(X).</math>

The image <math>\rho(G)\sub \operatorname{Sym}(X)</math> is a [[permutation group]] and the elements of <math>G</math> are represented as permutations of <math>X</math>.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1SPjBwAAQBAJ|title=Permutation Groups|last=Dixon|first=John D.|last2=Mortimer|first2=Brian|date=2012-12-06|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9781461207313|pages=5&ndash;6|language=en}}</ref> A permutation representation is equivalent to an [[Group action (mathematics)|action]] of <math>G</math> on the set <math>X</math>:

:<math>G\times X \to X.</math>

See the article on [[Group action (mathematics)|group action]] for further details.

==Linear permutation representation==
If <math>G</math> is a [[permutation group]] of degree <math>n</math>, then the '''permutation representation''' of <math>G</math> is the [[group representation|linear representation]] of <math>G</math>
:<math>\rho\colon G\to \operatorname{GL}_n(K)</math>
which maps <math>g\in G</math> to the corresponding [[permutation matrix]] (here <math>K</math> is an arbitrary [[field (mathematics)|field]]).<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BFrTBwAAQBAJ|title=A Course in the Theory of Groups|last=Robinson|first=Derek J. S.|date=2012-12-06|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9781468401288|language=en}}</ref> That is, <math>G</math> acts on <math>K^n</math> by permuting the standard basis vectors.

This notion of a permutation representation can, of course, be composed with the previous one to represent an arbitrary abstract group <math>G</math> as a group of permutation matrices. One first represents <math>G</math> as a permutation group and then maps each permutation to the corresponding matrix. Representing <math>G</math> as a permutation group acting on itself by [[Group (mathematics)#translation|translation]], one obtains the [[regular representation]]. 

==Character of the permutation representation==
Given a group <math>G</math> and a finite set <math>X</math> with <math>G</math> acting on the set <math>X</math> then the [[Character (mathematics)|character]] <math>\chi</math> of the permutation representation is exactly the number of fixed points of <math>X</math> under the action of <math>\rho(g)</math> on <math>X</math>. That is <math>\chi(g)=</math> the number of points of <math>X</math> fixed by <math>\rho(g)</math>. 

This follows since, if we represent the map <math>\rho(g)</math> with a matrix with basis defined by the elements of <math>X</math> we get a permutation matrix of <math>X</math>. Now the character of this representation is defined as the trace of this permutation matrix. An element on the diagonal of a permutation matrix is 1 if the point in <math>X</math> is fixed, and 0 otherwise. So we can conclude that the trace of the permutation matrix is exactly equal to the number of fixed points of <math>X</math>. 

For example, if <math>G=S_3</math> and <math>X=\{1, 2, 3\}</math> the character of the permutation representation can be computed with the formula <math>\chi(g)=</math> the number of points of <math>X</math> fixed by <math>g</math>.
So 
:<math>\chi((12))=\operatorname{tr}(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0\\ 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix})=1</math> as only 3 is fixed
:<math>\chi((123))=\operatorname{tr}(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix})=0</math> as no elements of <math>X</math> are fixed, and 
:<math>\chi(1)=\operatorname{tr}(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix})=3</math> as every element of <math>X</math> is fixed.
